label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Re: Finance wants to scrap salary advances completely. Am I wrong to push back?**

Peter, I respect where you're coming from, and nine years running payroll is more than most of us in this thread have. You're right about the people who take an advance every single month, and you're right that an informal arrangement where HR is the lender of first resort isn't healthy. But we did almost exactly what you're recommending, and we had to reverse it within seven months. Brenda asked whether anyone has actually tried closing the window, so here is how it went for us.

Some context. I'm HR at a logistics company, about 340 staff across two depots, one in Embakasi and one in Changamwe in Mombasa. Most of our people are drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks, so a similar pay profile to yours, Brenda. Our advances used to look like yours: informal, someone comes to my office, supervisor agrees, payroll pays out early. No written limit.

In early 2025 Finance pushed back with almost word for word the argument Peter has made. We're not a bank, it disrupts the forecast, some people are permanently a month behind. I didn't have numbers to counter it, so in February 2025 we closed it. We gave two months' notice, pointed people to the SACCO, and ran a financial literacy session with them. On paper we did everything properly.

**What happened in the six months after**

People didn't stop needing money. They went to the loan apps, which is what Brenda is worried about.

- Calls from debt collectors and loan apps to the office went from a handful to **61 logged by reception** in six months. That's only the ones reception wrote down.
- Some apps were calling **supervisors** because staff had listed them as "referees" when they signed up. So a private debt became a workplace problem. Supervisors were embarrassed and annoyed, and a couple of them started treating the people concerned differently. That ended up on my desk anyway, just as an employee relations issue rather than an advance request.
- Unplanned absence on the **two days after month-end** went up noticeably.
- Our fleet manager linked **at least three missed Mombasa runs** to drivers who were off "sorting out" loans. If you know logistics, you know what a missed run costs once you add the customer, the rescheduling and the overtime to cover it.

The case that changed my mind completely was a loader at Changamwe. By the time he came to me he had six apps running at once and was borrowing from one to pay the other. It took us **four months** with payroll to unwind it. That's a lot of HR and payroll time, which is exactly what Peter says advances waste. The difference is that this time was unplanned and nobody was budgeting for it.

**On the SACCO and financial literacy**

I'm not knocking either. Our SACCO is good and the literacy session was worth doing. We still run them. But a SACCO loan for us takes two to three weeks to process and needs guarantors. That's no use to a mother whose child is sent home over school fees on a Tuesday. She needs the money by Wednesday morning.

The literacy training also only goes so far when someone is on around KES 28,000 a month. You can teach budgeting very well, but at that income there isn't much room for an emergency fund. The emergency comes before the savings do. So the real choice isn't between an advance and the person managing without. It's between an advance and a loan app at whatever rate they're charging, with the collectors calling your supervisors.

On Peter's point that the apps are the employee's own decision and their own contract: in a legal sense, yes. In practice, it came back to us through the referee calls, the absence and the missed runs. The company was paying for those loans either way. We just weren't measuring it.

**What we did instead**

We reopened in **September 2025**, but as a written policy this time. That's the part I'd really encourage you to take into the meeting on the 18th, Brenda, because it deals with most of what your Finance Manager is worried about, including the people who were advancing every month.

The bones of it:

1. **Cap: maximum 40% of net pay.** Not gross. Net.
2. **Frequency: once per pay cycle.** No second advance in the same month.
3. **Repayment: in full at the next payroll.** No spreading it over several months, so nobody carries a rolling balance.
4. **No fee and no interest.** We're not trying to make money from it.
5. **Approval route: requests go through the payroll portal, not my office.** This matters more than I expected. It took the begging-at-the-door element out of it, it means I'm not making judgement calls about whose emergency is real, and it saves me a lot of time.
6. **Deductions check.** Before approving, payroll checks that total deductions, including the advance recovery, stay within the two-thirds limit under the Employment Act. That way nobody gets to month end with nothing in their account, which is the trap Peter is rightly worried about.

**Our numbers since reopening**

- About **55 to 70 requests a month**, averaging around **KES 9,000** each.
- **100% recovered except for two leavers.** Total written off for the year is roughly **KES 14,000**.

Peter, on recovery from leavers, you're right that it happens, but this is the real size of the problem for us. KES 14,000 across a year on a 340-person workforce. One missed Mombasa run costs us more than that.

The part your Finance Manager may find most interesting, Brenda, is that **ours now defends the scheme himself.** His objection was never really to advances. It was to not knowing. With a fixed ceiling he can forecast it. Worst case is roughly 40% of net pay for whoever applies, it all comes back next cycle, and there are no surprises. Kiprono said the same thing earlier: Finance stopped complaining once they could see a ceiling.

**How I'd frame it on the 18th**

If I were going in, I'd try to move the conversation away from "advances: yes or no" and towards comparing the costs side by side.

On one side, the cost of a formal scheme. Payroll admin time, the cash that's out for at most one cycle, and write-offs. All of this sits in one place and is easy for Finance to see, which is why it looks like the bigger problem.

On the other side, the cost of closing it. Absence after month-end, lost productivity, supervisors fielding collector calls, HR time spent untangling app debt, and in your case probably line downtime instead of missed runs. These costs are spread across departments, so nobody adds them up, and that's why they're easy to underestimate.

If you have any data at all, bring it. Absence by day of the month, how many advances you did last year and what was actually lost. You may find the losses are smaller than Finance assumes. Even if you only have our numbers, they show what happened when a similar workforce tried closing it.

I'd also give your Finance Manager the win on the repeat users. The informal system clearly isn't working. Propose replacing it rather than scrapping it: written rules, a hard cap, once a cycle, full repayment next payroll, an application route that doesn't go through you personally, and a deductions check. Then offer a six-month review with agreed measures, so he isn't being asked to take it on faith.

Peter, I don't think we're as far apart as it might look. We agree that informal advances with no limits are a bad idea, that HR shouldn't be a bank, and that the SACCO and financial education matter. Where I disagree is the idea that people adjust after one or two pay cycles. Ours didn't. They found other lenders, and those lenders were much worse for them, and in the end for us too.

Happy to answer anything else before the 18th, Brenda. Good luck.
